description: What each shipped saved search should return when the app is deployed against sample_events/. Generated numbers come from the same run_pipeline the determinism tests call; the expected-empty entries are stated with the reason, because a search returning nothing is the failure mode this whole app is careful about and it must be possible to tell a correct empty from a broken one.
corpus: tests/morpheus/determinism/estate_pipeline.py, lineage_pipeline.py, network_pipeline.py, transport_pipeline.py, presentation_pipeline.py, application_pipeline.py and session_pipeline.py, rendered through SiemWireStage by make_sample_events.py

R-D-L1-001 - Transceiver substitution.why: One port. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/2's serial changed at minute fifty, from XCVR-sw1-Gi1/0/2 to XCVR-sw1-Gi1/0/2-B, on a poll whose link_flaps is 0: oper_status read up on both polls and the device's ifLastChange never moved, so the device says the link was never down, which replacing an optic cannot avoid. The other optic replaced this hour, on hq:sw1:Gi1/0/6 at minute forty-five, is quiet: its serial changed just the same, but ifLastChange advanced between the two polls and TC1FlapStage counted the drop (link_flaps=2, link_flap_unpolled=true), which is what a swap looks like. The notable names both serials, the replaced one carried from the port's preceding poll.

R-P-L1-004 - Optical degradation forecas.why: One port, the one whose optic was failing. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/6's receive level slid 0.04 dB every poll from the start of the hour until the swap at minute forty-five; the line TC1ForecastStage fits through its readings falls about 58 dB a day, and from the twelfth poll on the stage projects it reaching the 10GBASE-LR floor of -14.4 dBm within hours. Thirty-four polls carry that projection, and the search's stats BY entity_key reduces them to one row carrying the shortest. Nothing else projects: the tapped port's three-decibel step reads not_degrading on the poll it lands, where the slope is still within the noise, and nonlinear on every poll after, where the readings no longer sit on a line; the steady ports' jitter never stands more than two and a half standard errors from flat against the bar of four; and the optic that replaces the failing one begins a history of its own, too short to fit for eleven polls and not degrading after.

R-D-L2-001 - MAC address count exceeded.why: The rule joins port_designations, which ships header-only. Until an inventory populates it the lookup returns nothing and the join yields nothing. 11 candidate rows carry macs_per_port_first_in_window=true, so a non-zero result after populating the lookup is the signal that the join works.

R-B-L2-002 - Port-to-MAC binding novelty.why: Two ports, the same two R-D-L2-001 would name if its designation list were populated, found without it. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/3 carried one address in each of the six snapshots before the hub arrived at minute thirty; the snapshot that carried the hub's four addresses raised its count to five, four above the most the port had ever carried, and each of those four rows is new to the window and a step. hq:sw1:Gi1/0/2 carried one address for nine snapshots and then the spoofed address beside it at minute forty-five, one above its own record. The search's stats BY port_key reduces the five rows to one notable per port. Every later snapshot on both ports has a baseline that absorbed the step, so the rule fires once per step rather than once per snapshot; and the peer switch's ports, which the estate met inside this hour, have no baseline to step above.

R-D-L2-003 - ARP anomaly.why: The search aggregates BY arp_sender_ip, so the 24 contested observations collapse to one notable for the one address that is contested by two MACs.

R-D-L2-004 - MAC in two places at once.why: One address claimed on a peer switch inside a single poll sweep (conflict, zero gap) and one displaced two seconds later. Both are inside the 60-second threshold. The roaming device, displaced a whole poll cadence later, is deliberately outside it.

R-D-L2-005 - Authorization without authe.why: One authorization on a port whose own exchanges were long finished, and one that arrived while a legitimate exchange on its port was still open. The second only appears because exchanges are keyed by device; keyed by port it would have paired with the innocent device's request.

R-B-L3-001 - Fan-out expansion.why: One notable, for the scanner. Two hosts in the corpus reach a comparable number of addresses and only one of them stays inside the estate: 10.0.0.50 reaches 5, 20, 45 and then 80 internal destinations in successive hours, and 10.0.0.60 reaches thirty on the public internet every hour and is not flagged. That is the whole of the difference between a scan and a lunch break, and it is why the rule requires the internal proportion as well as the count. The scanner_allowlist lookup ships header-only, so nothing is excluded here; populated, an authorized scanner would drop out. Note the threshold is a fixed dsts_per_src>50 standing in for the per-source fourteen-day percentile the guide asks for, which this app cannot compute without a history it does not keep.

R-B-L3-002 - Beaconing.why: One notable, for the pair 10.0.0.70:93.184.216.34, which exchanges a 512-byte message every five minutes for four hours. The negative control is 10.0.0.80, which makes plenty of flows to one file server at the ragged intervals a person produces and whose coefficient of variation is above 1.0 -- an order of magnitude above the 0.15 threshold. Grouped by flow_pair_key rather than by src_ip, because a host that beacons to one address and browses to five hundred others would have the beacon averaged away by a search keyed on the host. Five more pairs come from the campaign corpus, R-C-002's five hosts each sending a 512-byte message every sixty seconds; the rule reports all five on their regularity alone, and 40 more mature rows contribute.

R-D-L3-003 - Reserved-range egress.why: One flow, to 240.0.0.1. Low volume and high signal by nature, which is only true if the classification is right about everything else -- so what this number really asserts is that the other 410 flows are correctly classified as ordinary. The classification is parsers/ip.py's, through TC3ReachStage, so the search holds no copy of the reserved ranges.

R-B-L3-004 - TTL fingerprint shift.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.100, whose traffic starts arriving one hop short from the third hour onward: twelve flows, every one of them shifted by exactly -1, which is what a single interposed device costs. The control is 10.0.0.110, whose TTL never moves. The aggregate threshold of three shifted flows is what makes this a statement about a distribution rather than about a packet, which is what the guide's rule asks for; a single shifted flow is noise.

R-P-L3-005 - Fan-out trajectory.why: Empty, and for the same reason the chain assembly search is: it reads index=behavior_summary, which the Behavior summary saved search populates as it runs, and this package indexes pipeline output only. The trajectory is present in the data -- the scanner's fan-out rises 5, 20, 45, 80 across four consecutive windows, which is exactly the shape the rule reads -- so running the summary search first on a search head that keeps its output is what would make this fire. That is a deployment step rather than a corpus one.

R-D-L4-002 - SYN without completion.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.50, which sends a SYN to each of 60 destination ports inside one 60-second bin and is answered by none of them. The negative control is the workstation beside it, which opens connections to the same kind of ports in the same way and is answered: its flows carry three ACKs each and a syn/all of 0.14. The sweeper is a second control and a more interesting one -- every one of its SYNs is unanswered and scores exactly like the scanner's per flow, but it touches one port across thirty hosts rather than sixty ports on one, so a vertical-scan rule is right not to fire on it. 110 flows in the corpus satisfy the per-flow half of the predicate and one source satisfies the breadth.

R-D-L4-003 - RST ratio.why: Two notables from one predicate, which is the whole of this rule. 50 flows in the corpus carry refusals and nothing else, and they sit at the same rst/all of 0.5; what separates them is which side of the refusal fans out. 10.0.1.50 refuses 20 clients, which is a service outage and scores 10. 10.0.0.70 is refused by 30 servers, which is closed-port enumeration and scores 40. A rule reading only the ratio would return these as one kind of thing and send the wrong response to one of them.

R-B-L4-005 - Transfer envelope breach.why: One notable, for the triple 10.0.0.80:10.0.1.30:445, which transfers 60000 bytes against an envelope of 1200 -- fifty times its own 99th percentile. The negative control is 10.0.0.90:10.0.1.40:443, which moves more data in total and varies by a factor of two doing it: a global threshold would have to sit above the busy triple and would then sit above the exfiltration too. The envelope is a percentile rather than a maximum because the triple has 120 prior transfers, above the hundred a 99th percentile by nearest rank needs to be one; below that figure it would be the largest transfer ever seen wearing a percentile's name. Five more come from the campaign corpus: each of R-C-004's five actors' hosts uploads 1200 bytes to a sync server a hundred and ten times and then 60000 once, fifty times its envelope. The breach is identical in all five; whether the host belonged to the principal who had just exported, while their session held it, is what R-C-004 adds.

R-B-L6-001 - New TLS client fingerprint.why: One notable, for 10.0.0.20, which presented one TLS stack across 34 handshakes and then a second. The negative control is 10.0.0.21, whose second stack is equally novel the first time it appears -- it had made two handshakes at that point, so the settled-history floor of twenty separates them. That control is the one the corpus had to be rebuilt to show: novelty alone reports a host the estate has just started seeing exactly like a host whose stack changed. Four more come from the campaign corpus: R-C-002's attacker and three of its controls are settled hosts, twenty-four handshakes each, presenting a new stack once. The fifth control has five handshakes behind it and is held back by the floor, exactly as 10.0.0.21 is. Which of the four went on to beacon to the destination it presented the new stack to, within the hour, is R-C-002's to say.

R-D-L6-002 - Certificate issuer anomaly.why: Two notables, and the second is the interesting one. 93.184.216.34 presented a proxy's authority after a corpus of one corporate authority, which is interception. 93.184.216.36 migrated authorities legitimately, and the rule reports that once: the single-issuer gate closes on the next handshake, because the destination has now demonstrably presented two. The control is 93.184.216.35, a delivery host rotating among four authorities, which differs from its own mode on 19 handshakes and is removed entirely by the same gate.

key_values.presented_issuer: CN=Public Trust CA G3, O=Trust Services, C=US
key_values.established_issuer: CN=Public Trust CA G2, O=Trust Services, C=US

R-D-L6-003 - Self-signed to external des.why: One notable, for 93.184.216.37, over two connections carrying a self-signed certificate valid for three days. Eight handshakes in the corpus carry a self-signed certificate and six of them are the internal appliance at 10.0.1.50 -- a management interface nobody bought a certificate for, which is what an estate has hundreds of. The classification is parsers/ip.py's, through the same module TC3ReachStage uses, so the search holds no copy of the reserved ranges.

R-B-L6-004 - Cipher downgrade.why: One notable, for the pair 10.0.0.22:93.184.216.34, which negotiated modern suites ten times and then a broken one. Two controls: the varied host's conversations move between two sound suites routinely, which a reference taken as a mode rather than a minimum would have called a downgrade every time the weaker one was chosen, and the legacy appliance pair sits at a low floor permanently without ever falling below it.

R-D-L6-005 - Content type mismatch.why: One notable: an archive behind a declared PNG. 50 handshakes in the corpus carry both content types and reach the comparison, and 49 of them are re-encodings -- a declared PNG detected as a JPEG, which is a thumbnailer or a client guessing from the extension. A rule comparing types rather than categories would return all 50.

TLS table coverage - unrecognized values.why: One summary row, and the value is in the numbers rather than in whether it fired. Both zero here, which is what makes the five counts above mean what they claim: a corpus that had drifted outside the cipher ordering or the media type map would make those rules fire less and say nothing about why. In a real estate this is the search that reveals an inspection point emitting OpenSSL short names rather than IANA ones, which lands the entire cipher feed in unrecognized_ciphers.

R-B-L7-001 - DNS tunneling.why: One notable, for evil-tunnel.com: 130 distinct subdomains, every one of them random and long-labelled, from one client. Each of the rule's three conditions has a control in this corpus that it alone keeps quiet. cdn-assets.net clears entropy and the count and fails only on label length -- the guide's own warning that entropy alone flags every content delivery network. tenant-saas.com clears entropy and length on all 30 of its queries and fails only on the count, because it is one hostname asked for repeatedly; those 30 rows are why 160 rows clear the per-query conditions and only 130 contribute. saas-provider.com has 130 ordinary subdomains and fails both per-query conditions. The count is taken over qualifying queries in the search rather than read off the row, so all three conditions hold for the same traffic.

R-D-L7-005 - Enumeration.why: Two notables. 10.0.0.40 requested 220 distinct paths and was refused on nine in ten. 10.0.0.41 requested as many and was refused on every one, so its 4xx:2xx ratio is undefined on every row -- it appears only because the search tests 4xx > 0.7 * 2xx rather than thresholding the ratio column, and a search written the other way would lose the client the rule is most for. The crawler requests as many distinct paths and is refused on one in twenty; the broken client is refused on every request but asks for one path. Each fails exactly one condition.

R-D-L5-003 - Impossible travel.why: One principal is authenticated from New York half an hour after her own office login in London, and then back in London ninety minutes later. Two rows rather than one is what a single interloper produces: the jump away and the victim's next authentication from where she actually is. The traveller who makes the same crossing in eight hours is inside the threshold and does not appear, and the VPN user whose apparent location changes country twice a day is excluded by egress range rather than alerted on.

R-D-L5-004 - Multi-factor fatigue.why: Five denials at ninety-second intervals and then an approval: six challenges inside eight minutes, which clears both thresholds. The fumbled password beside it -- two failed authentications and a success, with the factor never challenged -- is failure-then-success with none of the denial volume the rule requires, and does not appear.

R-D-L5-007 - Off-hours authentication.why: Two successful sign-ins at an hour the principal's own mature histogram had never held. alice@example.com at 03:00 is the planted case, an office worker who has only ever signed in during office hours. bob@example.com at 08:00 is real too: the sign-in from London before his flight to New York, at an hour his office week never used. That is what the rule is for, and why it is a notable rather than a page. svc-batch@example.com signs in at 03:00 every night and does not appear: the same hour is ordinary in its own history, which is the negative control that makes the feature a statement about a principal rather than about a clock. carol@example.com's 02:00 burst is at an unseen hour as well, and is left to R-D-L5-004 and R-D-L5-009 because its rows at that hour are refusals until the last.

R-D-L5-008 - New authentication location.why: Two first sign-ins from a new place by principals whose history is mature. alice@example.com in New York is the impossible-travel row R-D-L5-003 also reports, from the other side: there the speed, here the place. bob@example.com in New York is his arrival after the flight, reported once and never again, because the set the stage keeps is cumulative. dave@example.com's first sign-in through the Frankfurt concentrator is also a new place, one prior sign-in into his history, and the cadence_mature gate keeps it out: in a principal's first days every place is new because nothing is old yet. No principal changes device in this corpus, so device_first_seen is never true.

R-D-L5-009 - Failed authentication run e.why: One run long enough to be guessing: carol@example.com's five refused attempts and then the approval. R-D-L5-004 reports the same burst from the factor's side, and two rules reading two columns of one event is correct rather than redundant. alice@example.com's fumbled password -- two failures and a success -- is failure-then-success below failure_threshold of 3, which is what most of an estate does on a Monday, and does not appear.

R-B-L5-001 - Composite authentication an.why: Correct, and for a reason the search states: it reads only rows whose model_fallback_used is false, and every scored row in this corpus was scored by the reference arithmetic under the manifest's fallback. A reconstruction error is a statement about a principal only when the model behind it was fitted to that principal. Nothing was tuned to make this empty -- without the gate it is empty too, because the reference scores reach a max_abs_z of 6.1 but never a mean_abs_z of 2.0. It returns rows once a trained per-user model is pinned in the manifest (issue #59).

R-B-L5-002 - Location novelty anomaly.why: Correct, for the same reason as R-B-L5-001: the search reads only rows a principal's own model scored, and every row here was scored under the fallback. Without the gate it is still empty, because the reference losses on locincrement peak at 1.4 against a threshold of 4.0. R-D-L5-008 asks the deterministic form of the question and returns its two rows today.

R-C-002 - TLS anomaly precedes beaconing.why: One chain, and the first time this rule has returned a row: it used to read the two detections' notables, which only exist once those detections have run, and now reads the scored events. 10.20.2.5, settled on one TLS stack across twenty-four handshakes, presented a new one to 203.0.113.100, and fourteen minutes later its beacon to that address matured. Four others do both halves with one condition broken and are quiet: 10.20.2.6 was already beaconing an hour before its new stack; 10.20.2.7's beacon went to a different address than its new stack; 10.20.2.8's beacon matured sixty-seven minutes later; 10.20.2.9 had five handshakes behind it, so its new stack is only new because the host is. Every one of the five beacons is an R-B-L3-002 notable, and four of the five new stacks are R-B-L6-001 notables, on their own.

Behavior summary - per-layer scores.why: One summary row per (five-minute bin, osi_layer, entity_key, lineage_id) over the 8205 scored events on `morpheus:score:l1` through `l7`. It was 320 before the estate pipeline rendered these events: the same layers 1 and 2, plus the desk authentications made in that hour, which add their own groups. `peak_z` is null on every row but layer 5's because only TC5ScoreStage produces `max_abs_z`; a null aggregate does not drop a row, so the count is a statement about the grouping, not about scoring coverage. The figures grew twice more as layers landed: layer 3 contributes 411 scored flows keyed on source addresses, layer 4 contributes 432 scored packets keyed on flows, layer 6 contributes 105 scored handshakes keyed on hosts, and layer 7 contributes 1180 DNS queries and HTTP requests keyed on the clients that made them, 1121 SaaS operations keyed on the principals who performed them and 1138 process starts keyed on the hosts that ran them, none of which shares an entity with the estate's ports and principals or with each other. The campaign corpus the chained rules are asserted on adds 308 flows, 82 host logins, 108 session records, 555 packets, 165 handshakes, 241 process starts and 555 SaaS operations on the layer 3 to 7 sourcetypes, sharing entities with one another and with no other corpus. The layer 1 figure grew by 61 rows and 13 groups when a sixth port joined the estate: the one whose optic is swapped with the link dropping, which is R-D-L1-001's control.

Chain assembly - cross-layer risk.why: Empty, and for a different reason than it has ever been empty before. The threshold this search was built around, `dc(osi_layer) >= 3`, is now met: 15 of the 3334 distinct `lineage_id` values hold a port's layer 1 samples, the layer 2 observations the ladder resolved onto that port, and the layer 5 authentications of the person sitting at it. The estate pipeline takes a `user_principal` through a supplied directory to a `dot1x_identity`, and through the 802.1X bindings to the port, and seals all three layers together. What stops the search is the line after it: `total_risk >= 60 OR (layer_span >= 4 AND peak_z >= 4.0)`. `risk_score` is written into the index by the detection searches as they fire, not by the pipeline, and this package indexes pipeline output only -- so `sum(risk_score)` is null for every chain, and no span reaches four. Running the detections first, on a search head that keeps their notables, is what would make this fire; that is a deployment step rather than a corpus or ladder one. Layer 4's arrival moved the denominator and nothing else: a flow is its own entity, so its 432 records carry 432 chains of one layer each, and Part 4's layer 3 to layer 4 hop is what would join them to anything. `methods` once read `join_method`, which no pipeline writes, and was blank on every chain; it now reads the `resolution_method` the binding resolver records, so all 15 three-layer chains say `soft:mac_table` and 60 chains in all carry a method.

Binding lookup - L2/L3 refresh.why: Empty, and the reason is the corpus rather than the search. This search selects binding_table=dhcp_lease, because several binding sources land on the one binding:bucketed sourcetype and a refresh that cannot tell them apart builds the wrong lookup. The 80 bucketed rows in binding_bucketed.jsonlines carry binding_table=mac_table: they are the layer 2 forwarding bindings TC2BindingStage closed, keyed on a MAC and resolving to a port, and binding_l2_l3 is keyed on an IP and resolves to a MAC. Nothing here speaks DHCP, so there is no lease to expand and the lookup this search builds stays empty. Pointing a DHCP feed at the pipeline and expanding it with to_bucketed_records(table_name="dhcp_lease") is what fills it; until then a zero here is the honest answer and the previous count of 80 was reading the whole sourcetype rather than the search's filter.

Binding lookup - L1 refresh.why: Seven port intervals across five ports: three stable, and two on each of the two ports whose optics are swapped partway through the corpus. Produced by TC1BindingStage from the TC-1 stream. The lookup is keyed on port_id and switch_id with no bucket, so a swapped port's two intervals collapse to one document and the row that survives is whichever the search wrote last -- which is why the search sorts ascending on bind_start before writing, making the surviving row the later optic rather than the earlier one. This lookup answers what is in a port now. What was in it on a given day is the history lookup below.

Binding lookup - L1 history refresh.why: Two rows, and two rows is the whole point. Of the five ports in the corpus only Gi1/0/2 and Gi1/0/6 have their optics replaced, so only their first intervals are superseded, and only superseded intervals are expanded into day-wide buckets by BindingTable.superseded(). The other three ports are described correctly for all time by the row the current-state lookup holds and cost nothing here. A number close to the port count would mean the superseded filter had been dropped and the history collection had started carrying the whole estate once per day.

Binding lookup - L1 history expiry.why: A maintenance search that deletes day buckets older than the retention window, the layer 1 twin of the L2/L3 expiry job. On a freshly loaded corpus nothing is old enough to expire, so an empty result is the correct one. Note that the current-state binding_l1 collection has no expiry job at all: it holds one row per port, and a decommissioned port's row is the last true thing known about it, so there is nothing there that grows.

Principal watchlist - expiry.why: A maintenance search that keeps only the watchlist entries whose expires has not passed. On a freshly loaded corpus the lookup holds what R-P-L5-006 and R-P-L7-006 have just written, and the events behind them are historical, so their thirty-day expiries are long past and the job drops every entry. The empty result is the job working; it is also why the expiry job must run after the predictive searches in a validation pass and not before R-B-L7-002 is checked.

Binding lookup - L2/L3 expiry.why: A maintenance search that deletes buckets older than the retention window. On a freshly loaded corpus nothing is old enough to expire, so an empty result is the correct one.

Binding health - unresolved rate.why: One row per sourcetype and telemetry class whose records carry a resolution outcome: the layer 1 port stream, the three layer 2 streams, and the campaign's host logins resolved through DHCP leases on layer 5. The search used to read morpheus:score:l3 alone, a sourcetype whose producer never writes resolution_method, so it could only ever return nothing; the retrospective's gap G24. The ARP stream's 180 unresolved of 1,220 is the corpus's planted rate (0.148), under the 0.2 that marks a class degraded. An operational metric: the value is in the numbers rather than in whether rows came back.

R-P-L5-006 - Drift trajectory.why: Six principal-days after deduplication, from 15 rows that carry the trajectory. None of them is behaviour, and the search says so in its own comment. Two principals climb for six straight days because the reference scorer's parameters are frozen while `logcount` and the `*increment` features are cumulative: a score whose baseline never moves under a feature that only grows must rise, and that is arithmetic. carol@example.com's day of the planted multi-factor burst used to fire as well -- a run of four whose first three rises are hundredths and whose fourth is the burst -- and the acceleration ceiling now keeps it out: its drift_acceleration is 0.81 against a ceiling of 0.1, while the two climbs accelerate by hundredths. A spike is R-D-L5-004's and R-B-L5-001's to report; drift is the slow climb no single day gives away. The predicate is evaluated here exactly as the search states it, so a corpus change that adds or removes a firing shows up as a diff rather than as a search that quietly means something else. What a deployment should take from this: the drift path's first false positives are cumulative features under a stale baseline, visible in `drift_baseline_sigma`. Every firing is also written to the principal_watchlist lookup, so after this search runs `| inputlookup principal_watchlist` holds six drift-trajectory entries for dave@example.com and svc-batch@example.com.

R-B-L7-002 - Bulk data access.why: Three notables, one per principal, and the classification sets each one's severity rather than deciding whether it fires. nate@example.com exported 5000 records from a restricted object against an export baseline of 54: 75. olga@example.com exported the same multiple from a public price list: 20. pat@example.com exported it from an object the inventory has never heard of: the default 40, with ctx_object_found=false. The controls each fail one condition: quin@example.com's 5000-record export is inside a baseline of 4978; sam@example.com's is 4.9 times theirs; rosa@example.com has twenty exports behind them and so no baseline; tom@example.com's export was denied and read nothing. nate@example.com also queries two to three thousand records all month, which is why the baseline is per operation -- pooled, the export would be under twice their normal. Five more come from the campaign corpus: each of R-C-004's five actors exports 5000 records against an export baseline of about 60, from an object no inventory in that corpus classifies, so each fires at the default 40. R-C-004 is what tells the one whose export was followed by a breach and a new issuer from the four that were not. The search also reads the principal_watchlist lookup and raises a watched principal's severity by 15, capped at 100. None of the eight is on the watchlist -- R-P-L5-006 watches dave@example.com and svc-batch@example.com and R-P-L7-006 watches ivy@example.com and kate@example.com -- so every severity here is the classification's alone. The weighting is asserted in test_saas_harness.py by putting a bulk exporter on the list.

R-P-L7-006 - Access breadth trajectory.why: Two principals watchlisted, evaluated over the whole corpus rather than the four-week dispatch window, which gives the same principals because every rise in it fits inside four weeks. ivy@example.com reached one more object type every week from week 3 to week 7 with the same group memberships throughout. kate@example.com did the same, and that principal's role did change in week 5 -- but the directory recorded it in week 9, so on every week of the rise the context attached to the operations said sales-users, and the rule could only know what was known. jack@example.com has the same rise with the same role change recorded on time, and is quiet because the memberships differ across the weeks. leo@example.com rises for two weeks only; mia@example.com reaches eight types every week and never rises. Both are written to the principal_watchlist lookup, one entry each, which R-B-L7-002 reads.

R-B-L7-004 - Process ancestry novelty.why: Four notables, and the integrity level sets each one's severity rather than deciding whether it fires. fin-01 started PowerShell from Word at high integrity, which nothing in the finance workstations' peer group had done in thirty days -- although the build servers do it every day, because another group is not a peer: 55. fin-02 ran a remote-access tool at system integrity that it last ran thirty-eight days earlier: 70. kiosk-01, which the inventory knows but has placed in no peer group, started mshta.exe: judged on its own history, endpoint_host_only=true, 40. build-02's git started curl with no integrity level reported: the default 40, with endpoint_integrity empty. The controls each fail one condition: build-02 compiled with a pair it had never run and its peer runs daily; fin-03 started an editor installed under a different user's profile than the peer who runs it, and per-user folders are collapsed; kiosk-01 started Notepad, which it last ran on day 20; lab-01, four days old and not in the inventory, started nmap before any comparison was possible. Six more come from the campaign corpus, on the servers its seven actors reached: each of six started a process no server in the group had run, at system integrity, 70 apiece, and the seventh started only what its server always runs. This rule cannot tell the one of them that followed a fan-out and a first login from the five that did not; R-C-001 is what does.

R-C-001 - Lateral movement chain.why: One chain, and the first chained rule in this app to return a row, because it reads the scored events rather than other rules' notables. From 10.20.0.5, fan-out rose above its own previous hour -- to twenty-five new addresses, half what R-B-L3-001 fires on -- then dana@example.com logged in from that address to SRV-DB-02, a server they had never logged into, and seven minutes later srv-db-02 started a process no server in its peer group had run in thirty days. Six other actors each do all of that but one step, and are quiet: the new process ran before the login; the last step came thirty-five minutes after the first; the login was to the principal's own server; the login came from another address; the fan-out was a busy host's steady twenty; the server only ran what it always runs. Five of those six processes are R-B-L7-004 notables on their own.

R-C-004 - Staged exfiltration.why: One chain. kim@example.com exported 5000 records, eighty times their own baseline; twenty-five minutes later the address kim's session held open, 10.20.1.5, sent 60000 bytes to its sync server, fifty times that triple's envelope; and twenty minutes after that it connected to a destination presenting an issuer nobody in the estate had seen in thirty days. Four others each do all three with one relation broken, and are quiet: lee's breach and connection came from the address max's session held; nia's came twenty minutes after nia logged off; oto's connection presented the corporate issuer every host sees daily; pia's breach and connection happened before the export. Every one of the five exports is an R-B-L7-002 notable and every breach an R-B-L4-005 notable on its own.

R-C-005 - Credential replay across the s.why: One principal. quin@example.com signed in at headquarters from 10.30.1.11 and, twenty minutes later, from 10.30.2.21; the DHCP leases name the two workstations behind those addresses and the MAC bindings closed from the two sites' switches put them at hq:hq-sw1:Gi1/0/11 and edinburgh:edi-sw1:Gi2/0/21, 534 km apart, which is 1601 km/h. Five others fall one step short and are quiet: rhea's two ports are both at headquarters; sam reaches Edinburgh three hours later, at 178 km/h; tia's second address is not one any lease names, so no port can be claimed for it; uma's was leased to an Edinburgh desk until an hour before the sign-in; and vic's second attempt was refused. None of the six is a geolocation alert: every sign-in carries a resolved port or none.
